blocks.title: This router cannot be automated yet
What to do
lines: PPPoE dialing and WAN Binding both write to the router, so neither is offered until the router answers for everything they depend on.
The OpenWRT Module settings page lists every check with what it costs. Once this blocking problem is cleared it also offers to install the missing packages it knows how to install.

blocks.title: Waiting for the router
lines: Automation appears here as soon as the router answers over SSH. Nothing is wrong yet - the readiness checks have simply not run.

blocks.title: Automation is held back until the probe answers
lines: The machine is connected and the readiness probe is running. Nothing has been read off the router yet, so the batches and binding instances below would be drawn against no sample at all - and both create forms would refuse anyway, because neither can tell what this router supports.
The probe repeats about every thirty seconds while this page is open. Check now asks immediately; if it never gets past this, Module settings names what the router is failing to answer.

blocks.title: Compatibility mode: no Bored Manager agent on this router
lines: Everything on this page is real and everything below still works. The module is driving the router over SSH, the way it always has.

What is missing is the safety net. A change that takes the connection down cannot undo itself, because there is nobody left on this side to tell it to; DHCP leases are read on a timer rather than as they happen; and a large PPPoE pool is written one round trip at a time.
Module settings, under Router packages, installs it - from a file on this machine when the router has no internet of its own.

blocks.title: Part of this page may refuse to run
lines: Something optional is missing. Creating a batch or a binding instance will say so with a specific reason; OpenWRT Module settings names it and installs it where it can.

blocks.title: Nothing on this page is being acted on
lines: WAN Binding reconciles on the fast probe, and the fast probe has stopped producing samples. No device is being assigned, no lease change is noticed, and no failed WAN is remapped until it recovers. The session and assignment tables below are the last good reading.
Reason below is what the last attempt returned. Refresh now, on either tab, retries immediately; if it keeps failing, check that the machine entry is still connected over SSH.

blocks.title: Session and WAN state below may be out of date
lines: The rest of the fast probe is answering, but the interface dump came back unreadable and the module is keeping the last list it could parse. Every PPPoE session state, every WAN state and the free-WAN counts each binding instance reports are read from that old list.
A session that has since dialled still reads as dialing, and a WAN that has since failed still reads as available - so binding can hand a client a WAN that is already down.

The usual cause is a pool large enough that the dump no longer fits in one answer. Raising the fast interval, in Settings, General, Update intervals, or shrinking the managed pool is what clears it; the module retries on its own every few ticks.

rows.label: Age of the last fast sample

blocks.title: How pools behave
lines: A pool is one carrier and a list of VLANs; each VLAN dials its own PPPoE session with its own routing table and, in shared-account mode, its own derived MAC. The router owns all of it: bm-pppoe-pool derives the interfaces, the tagged devices and the firewall zone from the pool record and reconciles them on every change.

Every member always has a row. Unwritten means the record names a member whose interface section is missing on the router - a create that stopped part way, or a section removed by hand. Applying any edit to the pool writes exactly the difference and repairs it.
Disable stops a session and keeps it stopped across reboots; Stop is the one-off. The router's own watchdog redials sessions that stay down - its timing is under Daemon settings.
Editing a pool applies to every interface in it in one pass. The check runs on the router and its findings are the same sentences LuCI and bmpppoe show.

blocks.title: The router stopped answering
lines: Everything below is the last answer the pool daemon gave. Nothing has been forgotten - the pools live on the router - but nothing here is live until it answers again. Refresh now retries immediately.

These were created by an earlier release as numbered session runs. This release neither edits nor watches them: delete each one and create it again as a pool of VLANs. Deleting removes its interfaces exactly as the release that made them would have.

blocks.title: Derived, read-only
lines: Interface names derive from the prefix and the VLAN: prefix fpt, VLAN 101 is section fpt101 on kernel device pppoe-fpt101, dialling over carrier.101. Its routing table and metric are table base + VLAN.

With MAC mode auto, each tagged member is assigned 02:xx:xx:xx:VV:VV - hashed from the carrier MAC and the pool id, with the VLAN in the last two octets - stable across reboots and reconciles. The untagged member (VLAN 0) always keeps the carrier's own MAC.
The id, the mode and the prefix cannot change: every derived name embeds them. Delete the pool and create a new one to change them.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Label - Only for people; shown wherever the pool is.
Service name / Access concentrator / AC MAC address - PPPoE discovery filters. Empty means autodetect, which is right for almost every ISP.

Username and Password - The shared account. Only used by shared-account pools; per-VLAN pools carry accounts on the Members tab. An empty password keeps the stored one; changing it redials every session.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Members - The pool's whole member list; applying replaces it. A VLAN missing from the list is removed - its session taken down and its interface deleted - and a new one is added with its firewall membership in the same pass.
Shared-account pools list VLANs: ranges and numbers, like 101-150,200,0. VLAN 0 means untagged on the bare carrier, at most once per pool.

Per-VLAN pools list one member per line: VLAN, username, password - separated by a comma, tab, semicolon, pipe or spaces. A kept VLAN may leave the username or password empty to keep what is stored; a new VLAN needs all three. Lines starting with # are ignored.

blocks.title: High-risk fields
lines: Everything below redials the pool or moves what it owns. Changing the carrier redials every session on the new uplink. Changing the table base moves every routing table - binding rules pointing at the old ones go stray until bm-wanbind's next pass. Changing the MAC mode presents changed MACs to the BRAS. Extra pppd options are passed verbatim: a wrong word fails every session.
The check names the exact impact before anything is written.

options.label: auto - one derived MAC per VLAN
inherit - every VLAN keeps the carrier MAC

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: MTU - Empty uses the pppd default of 1492. Above 1492 needs an ISP that supports RFC 4638.
LCP echo failures / interval - Presume the peer dead after this many missed echoes sent this many seconds apart. Empty leaves pppd's default of 5 and 1.
IPv6 - Disabled is the pool default; Automatic negotiates when the ISP offers it.
Use ISP DNS servers - Off means the DNS servers field is written per member instead; it is ignored while this is on.
Default route - Each session installs its default route into its own routing table, which is what a binding rule points a client at.

Host-Uniq - Raw hex bytes; leave empty unless the ISP requires it. Inactivity timeout - seconds of idle before hangup, 0 keeps sessions up. PADI attempts and timeout - discovery retries; empty leaves pppd's defaults.

Carrier - The physical uplink every member dials over. MAC mode - auto derives 02:... per VLAN from the carrier MAC, the pool id and the VLAN, stable across reboots; shared-account pools require it. Table base - each member routes in base + VLAN. Extra pppd options - passed to pppd verbatim, for the options this form does not carry.

fields.label: Allow LAN to reach this zone

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Zone - 1-11 letters, digits or underscores. The pool's members sit in it by explicit membership, written and reconciled by the router's pool daemon; pools may share one zone, and changing it moves every membership - the old zone is removed when nothing else uses it.
Masquerade and MTU fix - What a WAN zone needs: SNAT and MSS clamping. On a shared zone the union of what its pools ask wins.
Allow LAN to reach this zone - Writes one forwarding from the LAN zone, so clients can actually use the sessions.

blocks.title: What deleting removes
lines: Every interface in the pool is taken down and its section removed, with its tagged VLAN device and derived MAC. Every routing table the members used stops being written. The pool's zone memberships are removed, and the zone itself goes when no other pool uses it and WAN Binding is not installed. The record is removed last, so an interrupted delete can simply be run again.
The router refuses while a bm-wanbind instance hands clients to this carrier, and this page refuses while a binding instance is running on it - stop the instance first, on the WAN Binding tab.
The accounts themselves are not touched; they live wherever the list came from.

actions.label: Delete this pool
actions.confirm: Delete the whole pool - every interface, VLAN device, routing table and firewall membership it owns? Anybody dialling through it loses their connection.

blocks.title: The pool daemon comes from Router packages
lines: Pools are owned by bm-pppoe-pool 2.x on the router. If the check below says the pool daemon is missing or too old, install or update the router packages from Module settings, Router packages - the form unlocks when the router answers with it.

blocks.title: Tagged, untagged, and shared accounts
lines: VLAN 0 dials untagged on the bare carrier; VLANs 1-4094 add an 802.1Q tag, and the upstream must answer on that exact VLAN - a wrong tag looks like a PADO timeout.
A shared account carries as many sessions as the ISP allows. Each VLAN presents its own derived MAC so the BRAS can tell them apart; try two or three VLANs before pasting the full list.
One account per VLAN is the safe mode: each line has its own login, and MACs may inherit from the carrier or derive per VLAN.
Nothing is written until the check passes and you apply. The check runs on the router itself and names every derived interface, table and MAC decision it would make.

fields.label: Allow LAN to reach this zone

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Mode - Fixed for the life of the pool; delete and recreate to change it.
Pool id - 1-31 lowercase letters, digits or underscores. This is what you delete it by. Label - only for people.
Carrier - The physical uplink; the router lists what qualifies. Prefix - 1-4 characters, fixed after create; interface names derive from it: prefix fpt, VLAN 101 dials as fpt101 on pppoe-fpt101.
VLANs - Ranges and numbers, like 101-150,200. VLAN 0 means untagged, at most once. Username and Password - the one account every VLAN dials with.
Table base - Each member routes in table base + VLAN; the pool records its own base on the router.
Service name, Access concentrator, AC MAC - PPPoE discovery filters; empty means autodetect.

MTU - Empty uses the pppd default of 1492; above 1492 needs RFC 4638. LCP echo failures/interval - dead-peer detection; empty leaves pppd's defaults. IPv6, ISP DNS, DNS servers, Default route, Host-Uniq, Inactivity timeout, PADI attempts/timeout, Extra pppd options - the same options LuCI's PPPoE form carries, applied to every member.
Firewall zone - Created and owned by the router's pool daemon; pools may share one. Masquerade and MTU fix shape it; Allow LAN writes one forwarding from the LAN zone.

options.label: inherit - every VLAN keeps the carrier MAC
auto - one derived MAC per VLAN

fields.label: Allow LAN to reach this zone

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Mode - Fixed for the life of the pool. Pool id, Label, Carrier, Prefix - as on the shared-account tab; the prefix is fixed after create.
MAC mode - inherit keeps the carrier's MAC on every VLAN; auto derives a stable per-VLAN MAC from the carrier MAC, the pool id and the VLAN.
Member list file / Members - One member per line: VLAN, username, password - separated by a comma, tab, semicolon, pipe or spaces; # starts a comment. The file wins over the pasted text.
Everything below the member list is the same set of options as the shared-account tab, applied to every member.

blocks.title: The router's own watchdog
lines: netifd retries a failing PPPoE session by itself, and it is better at it than anything polling from outside. The watchdog on the router is for the sessions netifd has given up on: anything down longer than the redial delay is taken down and dialled again, longest-down first, at most one batch per pass.
These numbers live on the router, in /etc/config/bm_pppoe, and apply immediately: the counter timer is re-armed and the next watchdog pass uses them.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Counter interval - 1 to 300 seconds. How often the router reads /proc/net/dev and corrects its session table.
Redial after - 0 to 86400 seconds. How long a session may stay down before the watchdog redials it; 0 turns the watchdog off and leaves every retry to netifd.
Redial batch - 1 to 500. The most redials one watchdog pass starts: a provider that has just dropped four hundred sessions does not want four hundred simultaneous reconnects from one router.

blocks.title: One LAN client, one WAN
lines: An instance owns exactly one logical LAN and one physical WAN carrier. Interfaces outside that pair remain independent.
A sticky client keeps its WAN by MAC address. Optional remapping moves it only after the WAN has stayed failed beyond the grace period.
A newly leased device is assigned a random free WAN; when none is free it waits in FIFO order. New instances are created under Create an instance on this tab.

blocks.title: Operational warning
lines: A waiting device deliberately has no internet: a catch-all unreachable route stops it leaking through the router's default WAN.
Pausing the fast OpenWRT interval pauses this automation.

blocks.title: Above roughly 1,000 clients, three limits are yours to raise

lines: At that size the check reports conntrack, neighbour-table and flow-offload findings. This module deliberately does not write them: they are router-wide sysctls, they affect every service on the box, and getting one wrong takes the router off the network rather than one instance.
The shell below runs on the router itself. The check names the exact values; set them in /etc/sysctl.conf so they survive a reboot.
The dnsmasq lease limits the same check reports are the exception - those the module can raise for you, by the checkbox on the create form below.

blocks.title: The LAN and the carrier are fixed
lines: Every client rule and the safety catch-all were installed for this exact pair, so changing either would leave rules on the router pointing at a subnet that is no longer behind this instance. Delete the instance and create one for the new pair instead.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Instance name - A display label only. It must be unique on this router.
Keep a device on the same WAN - Remember the WAN by client MAC and prefer it after a lease IP change or a reconnect. Switching it off drops the choices already remembered for this instance.
Remap after a WAN failure - When a WAN stays in error longer than the configured grace period, move its client to another free WAN. Both flags take effect on the next reconcile.

Only the devices whose WAN is not healthy right now - failing, dialing, still inside its warning window, or gone from the pool altogether. This tab is open by default because the other one re-reads every assignment on each update, and only the tab you are looking at is fetched.

blocks.title: Why this is offered here
lines: This router is missing a package this automation depends on. The form below checks before it writes, so a create here would refuse and name it - and naming it, then sending you to another page, is a longer way round than doing it.

It is the same flow as Module settings: the check reads free space and whether the router has a route to the internet and changes nothing, and only names from this module's own fixed list ever reach a command line.
Applying runs a job and then re-reads the router. What that re-read finds is what unlocks the form.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: PPPoE support (ppp, ppp-mod-pppoe, kmod-pppoe) - What the PPPoE batch form below needs. A group already present is skipped.
Policy routing (ip-full) - What the WAN Binding form below needs. Some targets ship the BusyBox applet, which has no ip rule subcommand at all.
DHCP leases (dnsmasq) - Where WAN Binding finds the devices it assigns. Without it the device table stays empty.

fields.label: Keep a device on the same WAN
Raise dnsmasq lease limits when needed

blocks.title: Both forms check before they write
lines: Check reads the router and changes nothing. It reports what apply would do and refuses outright when the router cannot support it; only then does the apply button unlock.
A check result is single-use and expires after ten minutes, and it is tied to the exact values that were checked - editing a field means checking again.

Applying starts a job. It writes to the router in bounded chunks and can be cancelled between them - whatever was already written stays on the router, and the module keeps only the part that committed.

blocks.title: The two select lists are read once, when this tab opens
lines: Physical WAN carrier, DHCP LAN interface and WAN carrier are all built from the last router sample. Before the first sweep lands they are empty, and an interface added since this tab was opened is not in them.
Refresh the router sample below, then leave this tab and come back: the lists are rebuilt each time the tab becomes visible.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Instance name - A unique display label for this one LAN and one carrier pair.

DHCP LAN interface - The logical OpenWRT interface whose IPv4 DHCP leases are assigned. It must have a subnet and a dnsmasq DHCP section; when dnsmasq itself is missing, Module settings can install it.
WAN carrier - A device, or one VLAN on a device when the ISP hands out the uplink tagged. Every PPPoE, DHCP, or static WAN using it, directly or through one of its VLANs, becomes part of the pool.
Keep a device on the same WAN - Remember the WAN by client MAC and prefer it after a lease IP change or a reconnect, when that WAN is free and healthy.
Remap after a WAN failure - When a WAN stays in error longer than the configured grace period, move its client to another free WAN.

Raise dnsmasq lease limits when needed - Allow apply to raise this LAN's DHCP limit and the global dnsmasq lease cap to the size the check reports. That restarts dnsmasq, which briefly interrupts DHCP and DNS for the whole router; leave it off and the check still reports the numbers to set by hand.

blocks.title: What each field means
lines: Remap after WAN errors - default on for new instances when no per-instance value is supplied. Each instance’s own Remap choice is authoritative afterwards.
WAN error grace - 0 to 3600 seconds, default 30. A failed WAN must remain failed this long before its client can move.
New-WAN warning window - 0 to 3600 seconds, default 60. A newly reconnected WAN stays Warning for this long so flapping is visible.
Sticky by MAC - default on for new instances when no per-instance value is supplied. Each instance’s own Sticky choice is authoritative afterwards.
Lease release grace - 0 to 86400 seconds, default 300. The WAN stays reserved for this long after a DHCP lease disappears.
Watchdog redial after - 0 disables the watchdog (default) because netifd already retries. A positive value redials sessions that stay failed for that many minutes.

Repair WAN routing tables automatically - default on. When a managed WAN loses its option ip4table, rewrite it and reload the network. Switch it off to keep every write to /etc/config/network under your own hand; the audit still runs and reports what it found under Events.
DHCP lease file - default /tmp/dhcp.leases. An absolute path without shell metacharacters, in dnsmasq’s standard lease format.
These are the defaults new instances start from. An instance that already exists keeps its own Sticky and Remap, editable from its row.

blocks.title: Bounded background work
lines: A running job lives in memory and cannot resume after the app restarts. Reconciliation repairs whatever router state that leaves behind.
Cancel stops the steps that have not started; a command already running on the router is allowed to finish.
A step can also finish as a warning: the router took the change and then did not show it. The job carries on, and the warning is kept in the history.

blocks.title: What lands here
lines: Everything the automation decided on its own: a device bound or moved, a session created or deleted, a firewall rule that verified empty, a watchdog redial, a router reboot the module recovered from.

Binding events belong to one instance and also appear in that instance's own drawer on the WAN Binding tab. PPPoE and router events belong to the router rather than to any instance, so this table is the only place in the app that shows them.
The list is bounded per router, so the oldest entries are dropped. Nothing here ever carries router command output, because a rejected uci line can contain a PPPoE password.
